_comment: Source register for the Preparedness Archive. 'verified_on' is set ONLY when the page was fetched and its relevant content read on that date. 'human_link_check' stays false until a person has clicked through. Entries with verified_on=null are listed in Issue #136 as starting points and must not be cited in an article until verified.
verification_method_note: 2026-10-29 verification = machine fetch of the live page via Firecrawl scrape (maxAge 0) and reading of the returned text by the drafting agent. Not yet a human click-through.

sources.title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days; try for 2 weeks; more for pregnancy, illness, pets, heat; container cleaning (1 tsp unscented bleach per quart, 30 seconds); replace stored water every 6 months; unscented bleach 5-9% sodium hypochlorite.
sources.notes: Page metadata also shows a 2026-04-24 republish; the visible 'Updated/Reviewed' date is 2025-06-27.

sources.title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Boil 1 minute (3 above 6,500 ft); clear cloudy water first; bleach tables (5-9% and 1%); wait 30 minutes; chemical disinfectants weaker against Cryptosporidium and Giardia; chlorine dioxide tablets vs Cryptosporidium; iodine cautions; filter pore sizes 0.3 and 1 micron, viruses not removed; UV and solar disinfection limits; cannot make water containing fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive materials safe by boiling or disinfecting; never drink radiator or boiler water.
sources.notes: Page metadata shows a 2025-12-18 republish; visible 'Updated/Reviewed' date is 2024-09-19.

sources.title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
sources.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Water)
sources.supports: Independent cross-check of CDC: boil at least 1 minute, 3 minutes above 5,000 ft; 8 drops of 6% bleach per gallon, double if cloudy/colored/cold, stand 30 minutes; do not use scented, color-safe or added-cleaner bleach; bleach stored at room temperature under 1 year; boiling/disinfection do not destroy heavy metals, salts and most chemicals; Safe Drinking Water Hotline 1-800-426-4791.
sources.notes: DISCREPANCY with CDC: EPA's high-altitude boiling threshold is 5,000 ft; CDC's is 6,500 ft. Page metadata lists a future review date (2027-02-24), which is a schedule, not a past review.

sources.title: Botulism Prevention
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Common botulism sources are improperly canned, preserved or fermented homemade foods; toxin cannot be seen, smelled or tasted; pressure canning is the only recommended method for low-acid foods; 'If in doubt, throw it out'.

sources.title: Clostridium botulinum & Botulism
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: Botulism has been linked to traditionally prepared salted or fermented fish; nitrites in cured meat inhibit C. botulinum spore growth; USDA authorized nitrite in meat and poultry beginning 1925; early-1970s nitrosamine concern; spores survive boiling, pressure needed for low-acid foods; symptoms and urgency.

sources.title: How do I safely cure meats at home to avoid botulism?
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
sources.supports: Many botulism cases followed home-canned, preserved, curing, smoking or fermented foods contaminated with toxin. Short article; it points to the NCHFP for method detail and gives no home curing formula.

sources.title: Curing & Smoking
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia, USDA-supported)
sources.supports: Describes curing as using salt (and sometimes sugar) to draw moisture from meat and discourage harmful microorganisms, and as a matter of balancing time, temperature and ingredients.
sources.notes: This is a topic index page with a short description, not a tested procedure. No curing formulas are taken from it.

sources.title: Food and Drink in the U.S. Navy, 1794 to 1820
sources.supports: 1813 provisions load-out and weekly ration table; 1812 Binney contract specification for beef and pork; steeping of salt meat; bread/biscuit contract and dimensions; 'hardtack' as a 1840s term; pests; water rules (1802 regulations); Porter on water casks. Cites primary records (NARA contracts, ship journals, Naval Regulations 1802) in footnotes.
sources.notes: Secondary study built on primary records. Its footnotes are the route to the primary documents; those have not yet been pulled individually.

sources.title: Life at sea in the age of sail
sources.supports: Main rations were salt beef or pork, cheese, fish, ale and ship's biscuit; food quality worsened with poor storage, ventilation and vermin; scurvy caused by lack of vitamin C.
sources.notes: Short overview with no quantities or dates for the ration.

sources.title: Ship's Biscuit (AAB0766)
sources.publisher: Royal Museums Greenwich, National Maritime Museum
sources.supports: A ship's biscuit made to an 1846 recipe, marked with a broad arrow and the letter C; wheat; measurements 15 x 135 mm; not on display.
sources.notes: Image rights are held by RMG (licensing offered). No RMG image is used in this archive.

sources.title: Life Aboard (On the Water: Fishing for a Living)
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.supports: Gloucester schooner Ocean King, 1879 Grand Banks voyage, cook George W. Scott's journal list of provisions for a four-month voyage, including 210 hogsheads of salt for salting cod, 5 barrels beef, 1 barrel pork, 1 barrel hams.

sources.title: A treatise of the scurvy, in three parts (James Lind, 1753)
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (digitized, no known copyright)
sources.supports: Digitized primary source: first published 1753; full text and PDF available through the Internet Archive item. Library catalogue note says more sailors were dying from scurvy than from combat when it appeared.
sources.notes: The drafting agent read the catalogue record, not the 456-page text. Page-level claims from the Treatise are NOT made in articles.

sources.title: James Lind and scurvy: 1747 to 1795
sources.publisher: The James Lind Library (Ulrich Troehler, 2003; republished J R Soc Med 2005;98:519-522)
sources.supports: Lind's 1747 comparison aboard HMS Salisbury (80 of 350 sailors struck by scurvy in a ten-week cruise; 12 patients, six treatments); Sick and Hurt Board rejected a fruit-juice proposal the year after the Treatise; 'rob' made by heating destroyed much ascorbic acid; 1795 Admiralty sanction of lemon juice; a lag the author counts as 42 years.

sources.title: Drinking Water Advisories: An Overview
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Three advisory types (boil water, do not drink, do not use) and what each asks of a household; do not use fridge water or ice dispensers during any advisory; boil tap water even if filtered; infant feeding, handwashing, bathing, brushing teeth, dishes (150 F dishwasher; 1 tsp unscented bleach per gallon soak), laundry, cleaning, pets, gardens; boiling does not fix chemicals or toxins; do-not-use advisories are rare.
sources.notes: The page's visible 'Updated' date (Feb 21, 2024) precedes its 'Published' date (Sep 16, 2024); both recorded as shown. Page metadata shows a 2025-06-25 republish.

sources.title: How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Other water inside the home (tap water heater tank, melted ice cubes, clear untreated toilet tank water, liquid from canned fruit and vegetables, pool/spa water for hygiene only); outdoor sources (rainwater, streams, ponds, springs) must be treated; contaminated-by-fuel-or-chemicals water cannot be made safe; may need to shut the main water valve.

sources.title: About Water Treatment Options When Hiking, Camping, or Traveling
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Clear water can be unsafe; boiling best; filter then disinfect next best; absolute pore sizes (1 micron parasites; 0.3 micron bacteria and parasites; viruses not removed) or NSF 53/58 cyst certification; reverse osmosis removes parasites, bacteria, viruses and salt; chlorine dioxide vs parasites; UV needs clear water; iodine cautions.

sources.title: Two Ways to Purify Water
sources.supports: Never drink untreated natural water even if clear; filtration by itself does not purify water and must be followed by boiling or disinfection; filters are screens that cannot remove viruses; filter cloudy water even if you will boil it; filter care per manufacturer; pool-cleaning tablets must not be used; consult a physician about iodine; boiling 1 min (3 min above 6,500 ft) works even on cloudy water; UV is for small quantities of clear water.

sources.title: Water
sources.supports: At least one gallon per person per day for drinking and sanitation; normal active person needs about three quarters of a gallon of fluid; more for children, nursing mothers, sick people, medical emergencies, warm climates (need can double); never ration drinking water unless ordered; avoid carbonated and caffeinated substitutes; bottled water in sealed original containers, cool and dark; replace non-commercial stored water every six months; settle or strain before treating; boiling; bleach 5.25-6% only (1/8 tsp per gallon); distillation removes microbes, heavy metals, salts and most chemicals.
sources.notes: DISCREPANCIES with CDC: Ready.gov limits bleach to 5.25-6.0% and says iodine and camping-store treatments 'are not recommended'; CDC accepts 5-9% bleach plus iodine and chlorine dioxide products. Page is older (updated 2021).

sources.title: Prepare Your Pets for Disasters
sources.supports: Pets belong in the household plan; two pet kits (shelter and evacuation); store a water bowl and several days' supply of water for pets; no per-pet water quantity is given.
sources.notes: No numerical pet water allowance in this source. Do not invent one.
